utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, everybody. May the case be called, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the appearances, please. The Prosecutor. In this case --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nicholas Koumjian, Kapila Waidyaratne, and Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I today at the beginning of the fourth week of our hearing, ask Dr. Stakic is there any personal problems, especially in the detention unit, any problems of health or something like that? At the beginning of the hearing, I said that I won't come back each and every day to this issue, but today, let me know. Are there any problems? THE ACCUSED STAKIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for inquiring. But for the time being, I don't have any problems. And due to that, I did not ask to speak up earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, feel free whenever you regard it as necessary to inform the Bench about problems arising. THE ACCUSED STAKIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Very brief, we have before us still the Prosecution's motion to amend the witness list. It was filed on a confidential basis. Therefore, maybe go for just a minute into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Muharem Murselovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated when you have taken the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor may start the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Muharem Murselovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: 24th of November, 1947.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where were you raised?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I completed my elementary and secondary schools in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak of Islamic faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said that you attended your elementary and secondary schools in Prijedor. Did you specialise in any specific area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. After completing my secondary school, I was trained in Opatija at the school for caterers and I completed my degree there. Opatija is currently located in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you teach at any school at any time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I used to work at the school for catering, because that was my trade, that was my specialty. I was a lecturer there, and I thought subjects in the field of catering.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, are you married?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I was married, and I have two adult children who are married now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where did you reside before the conflict in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I have spent my entire life in Prijedor. I have always worked there. I used to work at a school for a time, and then after that, I was engaged in a private business.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in the centre of Prijedor the entire time, in the main street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Is it number 43, Marsal Tito?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the number was 43. That's correct. Before the war, I lived in Marsal Tito Street, number 43. That's what it used to be called before the war. Now it's called the Street of Peter 1st, the Liberator. The number is still 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, did you own any restaurants or were you in the business of running restaurants?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have worked in catering my entire life. At the end of 1978, I opened a private restaurant that was called Mursel. That was my name, my nickname, in fact. This was how I was known and that's how people normally call me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where was this restaurant located?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The restaurant was located in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you give a brief description of the restaurant that you had before the war.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a restaurant with some 50 seats. It had one large room and a smaller parlour. And it was mainly frequented by businessmen. It served European dishes in addition to some local specialties. I tried to make it into a decent restaurant. People of various nationalities and people from all over Bosnia and former Yugoslavia used to frequent my restaurant. It was a restaurant that had many patrons, and I was quite busy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you also have a snack bar other than the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had another establishment. It was a snack bar. And it was quite a different establishment. I served fast food there, hamburgers, pizza, sandwiches and so on, cakes, and well, other food items that are appropriate for a snack bar. This snack bar was also located in downtown, in the pedestrian area in the street called Marsal Tito Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, before the conflict in Prijedor in 1992, could we say that you were a businessman of good standing, and well established?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as compared to the others, it was the time of socialist regime, and you could say that I had more than other people. But you couldn't call it -- you can't say that I was particularly well off. The establishments were owned by myself and my family. My late father was involved in a similar business for over 50 years in Prijedor as was my late mother. So I simply continued this family tradition, and perhaps you could say that by owning these two establishments and by owning my own apartment, that I was -- that I was well off as compared to the others. Of course, you couldn't say that I was well off as compared to the current times. Yes, my family and I owned more than other people in the past, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, before the conflict in 1992, did you sell the building and your -- the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I sold one building in which my restaurant Mursel was located, and an apartment -- rather two apartments above the restaurant. That was a move of mine that I can now analyse as a move expressing my desire to build something new, newer and better building. I spent some 13, 14 years in that restaurant, and I thought it was better for me to sell it than renovate it. It was quite logical for me to sell it and then perhaps invest in another one. And my thoughts were along these lines, and therefore I sold the entire building together with the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you were the owner of the house or the place that you resided before the war? You owned the building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everything was owned by myself and by my family. Some was owned by my mother, my late mother. Something was owned by my wife. But yes, everything was owned by my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you perform compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In the former Yugoslavia I completed my military service in 1969 and 1970. Part of my service I spent in Sisak, and the other in Crpia od Krki [phoen], that is near Zagreb, towards Ljubljana in Slovenia. It is a small town, and I served there for some time. I came back from the army in 1970 having spent there a bit less than one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you were a member of a political party under the multiparty system. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you tell the name of the party and during what time, what period this was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I was a private entrepreneur, an independent private entrepreneur, as we used to call it in those days. And after the multiparty system emerged, there were a number of political parties and we wanted to protect our own interests in that system in which the dominant force was the state capital. We wanted to create a party which would regardless of everything be able to protect the interests of us private entrepreneurs. And therefore, we established the party called the Party of Private Initiative. I was a member of that party. And during those first multiparty elections, I was elected for the first time to the Municipal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Assembly as a delegate of my party, and I became an assemblyman of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. That was at the end of 1989 -- sorry, at the end of 1990, this was when the first multiparty elections were held. This was when I became an assemblyman of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Other than becoming a deputy in the Municipal Assembly, did you hold any specific post in your own party?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think there might have been a misunderstanding. I was an assemblyman of that party in the Municipal Assembly. And in addition to, that I was an active member of that party, and I was its vice-president on the municipal level. But this is of less importance. I was also at the head of the list of my party, and as I said, I was elected an assemblyman in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, under the multiparty system, what are the other parties which is prominent in Prijedor during that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: After these first multiparty elections, the greatest, the largest parties that had their deputies in the Municipal Assembly, in addition to my party which was a small party and had only one assemblyman, so these larger parties were the SDA. That was the largest party. It had 30 assemblyman. Then we had Serbian democratic party known as SDS, which had 28 assemblymen. And there was also, if I can call it that, former socialist party which had something around 13 assemblymen. And then there was also the party called the Reformist Forces, that was the party of Ante Markovic. It had some 10 assemblymen. There was the HDZ there as well. It was a Croatian party, Croatian democratic party. It had only 2 assemblymen. So there was another party. It was called Democratic Socialist Alliance. I think it had 5 assemblymen. There was a total of 90 assemblymen in the party, and eight political parties represented there. I'm sorry, 90 assemblymen in the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you described the composition of the Municipal Assembly. Could you very briefly say, the prominent members, specifically in the party of the SDA under the multiparty system?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the names, the individuals who represented that party?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was professor Muhamed Cehajic, who was later elected as the president of the Municipal Assembly. He taught in the secondary school. Then there was a man called Music, Ilijas. He was a professor of physics. He taught at another secondary school for economic education. Then, there was also Meho Tursic, who used to be the president of the Municipal Assembly, and later on he was a director of the public accounting office. There was also a man called Talundzic, a man called Sarajlic. And there were a lot of people who represented the top leadership of that party. The chairman of the party was a physician, Mirza Mujadzic. There was a lot of people involved actively in the SDA. There was a man called Nijaz Kapetanovic. There were a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of one Mr. Becir Medunjanin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I cannot remember all of them. There were so many of them. Becir Medunjanin was a teacher at the elementary school, Rade Kondic in Kozarac. He was married to a woman in Prijedor. He lived in Kozarac. I know his family personally. He had two sons. He and his wife both worked at the school in Kozarac up until those multiparty elections. I knew him superficially as a teacher in that school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, now that you have given the names with regard to the people in the SDA, could you also recall the names of the prominent people in the Serbian party, the SDS during that time.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian democratic party the prominent members were Simo Miskovic who was chairman of the party at that time. Then Srdjo Srdic, then Milomir Stakic. Then Dr. Kovacevic. Slavko Budimir. There was also a large number of people there who were active in that party. There was a man called Timarac, who is deceased now from Omarska. He was also an assemblyman like Srdjo Srdic. There were assemblymen in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, you described the composition and the amount of -- the number of members which are selected to the Municipal Assembly. Could you describe whether you knew or whether you were aware of any agreements between the two -- three main parties before the elections?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a public secret that those three parties as we used to call them, three national parties, that represented their own peoples. So by this, I mean the SDA, the SDS, and HDZ. So it was rumoured that an agreement has been signed between them specifying that they will create a coalition, some kind of an informal alliance to divide power among them. This was an agreement before the elections. I think that in the beginning it was honoured in Prijedor as well. The people who held the positions were the people from the HDZ, the SDS, and SDA. And even though the HDZ was a small party that had only two assemblymen, it was a coalition partner in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Together these three parties had 60 out of 90 assemblymen, and the rest of the political parties were the so-called opposition, and they had a total of 30 assemblymen among them, and I was one of them, representing a small political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was the relationship that your party had with the other three main parties before the election and after the election?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: My political platform, the representatives of my political party, were all entrepreneurs, people representing those who were engaged in some kind of private business activity. Although I have to say that entrepreneurs were represented in other political parties as well, but I, myself, and my political party, believed that we would best be able to protect our interests in a multi-party election. This is why we decided to participate in the elections. Their attitude towards us as a small marginal party in view of the number of our deputies was the same as the attitude towards all other political parties who were in the opposition. We didn't count much, so to speak, and we did not participate in the allocation of functions in the assembly. This was done by these three main political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, before we go to another area, could you also tell briefly the -- how the allocations were done after the elections? Who held what post after the elections?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I have already said, the SDS and the SDA, together with the HDZ, which had only two assemblymen but was participating in the division of power, because this was their previous agreement, they between themselves agreed to divide and allocate the functions among them. So this allocation of functions in the assembly was agreed upon between them before. They came out with this in the assembly, and that was adopted. I don't know whether between themselves there were frictions regarding this allocation, but the most important position, the president of the municipality, was awarded to the SDA, because that party had the largest number of the assemblymen. And it was logical for that party who had the largest body of voters and the largest number of assemblymen, it was logical for them to be given this position of the president of the municipality. That was quite normal. The position of the vice-president, which was second ranking position, was allocated to the SDS and Milomir Stakic, president of the executive council, as an office that had to coordinate contacts with enterprises, with various departments and divisions of the Municipal Assembly, was given to Dr. Kovacevic, also a member of the SDS. Becir Medunjanin became the secretary of the municipal secretariat for people's defence. This is what this body was called. Therefore, Medunjanin became the secretary of the secretariat. So these most important positions were allocated between these two most important political parties, with HDZ be given some smaller functions so that everybody was happy. And they had this proposal, or rather they came out with this proposal, and if I remember correctly, we voted on it and adopted it and this is how it became implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in that previous answer, you said the most important position, the president of the assembly, was given to the person from the SDA, Mr. Cehajic. Could you explain what functions did the president of the Municipal Assembly perform under that multi-party system?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that kind of system, I have to say that this was inherited from the previous regime, and unlike what we have today, the president of the municipality was a complete authority. He not only chaired the assembly sessions, but was also superior to everybody else in the municipal administration. Therefore, this person represented also the legislative and the executive power. And this person had power over all secretariats, all departments of the municipality of municipal administration. That person was in charge of hiring and firing employees, Was in charge of the budget, approving, adopting the budget. Therefore, the president of the municipality had a dominant role, and he was assisted in his work as the vice-president of the municipality, who was the president's closest assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Further, Mr. Murselovic, did the Municipal Assembly coordinate or cooperate with the police?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The then organisation of the police which at that time was known as the Secretariat of the Interior, or SUP, was directly subordinated to the municipality. It was a municipal body just like all secretariats in the Municipal Assembly, but in terms of its professional competences, it was also subordinated to the ministries and had to coordinate its work with the ministry. But at any rate, the secretary of the secretariat of the interior was an important position. And after multi-party elections, Hasan Talundzic was appointed to that office as a prominent member of the SDA. I remember that it was said that that was the first Bosniak who was appointed to that position after the Second World War. He was the first Muslim and Bosniak to be appointed to that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, with the time passing, in approaching 1992, what was the working relationship within the coalition government that was functioning at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is generally believed that these three parties were able to find common ground only when it came to bringing down communists. And this is what they did. This is where they were in unison. However, as the time passed, these so-called partners developed many antagonisms, and this was a heavy burden for the work of the municipality. I think that these were simply two political options that were unable to work in harmony. It is impossible to reconcile them. And as the time passed and as we got closer to 1992, these conflicts within the municipality and within the parties in power became more and more evident. And we could say that by the time -- by 1992, nothing functioned properly any more. The assembly sessions were scheduled. However, they were frequently adjourned, and the sessions were interrupted and discontinued because we were unable to adopt decisions and do all the business that is normally within the sphere of Municipal Assembly's responsibilities. It became obvious that there were many disagreements between the SDS and the SDA in many areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, during this time at the beginning of 1992, do you remember the establishment or proclamation of the Serbian municipality which was formed in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of 1992, after several interruptions in the work of the Municipal Assembly, there were arguments and the demands in favour of the assembly taking a stance on an issue. And we perhaps might say here that the most important point of friction was that the SDA wanted to pass a resolution about remaining in the federal state of Yugoslavia. But it was not a matter for the municipality to deal with, but there were interruptions and blockings of the work of the assembly. And regular work of the Municipal Assembly simply could not evolve. There were many blockades in the work of the assembly. In early 1992, a Serbian municipality of Prijedor was set up. There were Serbian deputies, deputies of the SDS there, and they proclaimed that part of the assembly which numbered 90 people, they proclaimed them the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor -- Serbian assembly of Prijedor. And this, of course, was an abnormal situation, it was abnormal to ask that this be a Serbian municipality when the municipality counted a larger number of Bosniaks. According to the 1991 census of the 12.000, there were 44 per cent Bosniaks, 42.5 were Serbs, and 5.6 Croats. There were also Yugoslavs and others who pronounced themselves as national minorities, so that the Serb deputies wanted to proclaim the Serbian municipality of Prijedor, which was done officially. And from my point of view, this was funny, ridiculous. It was a mixed municipality. There were not on one side Bosniaks and on the other side Serbs. They were mixed. They were intermingled. There were Bosniak, Serb villages, Croat villages, and to proclaim it a Serb municipality, I think is ridiculous. But this is, in fact, what happened, and at that assembly of the Serb municipality of Prijedor, they proclaimed all leaders in the Prijedor municipality who were in some way necessary, the vice-president, president, secretaries, heads of department, the presidents of the courts -- I apologise. At the Serb municipality of Prijedor which was proclaimed in early 1992, I think it was in February of 1992, the Serb deputies proclaimed that municipality as a Serb municipality, and they appointed all the officials who, true enough, coincided with some of them who were in power at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, I would please request you to speak slowly, because the interpretation would be much easier then. And also, do you know as to what post was held by Mr. Stakic in that Serbian municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was appointed president of the Serb municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Who were the other people who held the prominent posts or positions in that formation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the president of the courts, of the judiciary, there was Kreca Mico, president of the executive council remained Dr. Kovacevic who -- then Simo Drljaca was appointed head of the secretariat for internal affairs of the interior. Budimir, Slavko was appointed secretary of the municipal secretariat for defence, and so on. So they appointed parallel bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, how did you get to know about this? What was the source or how did you get to know the information about this Serbian -- all-Serbian municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in the mass media, in the Kozarski Vjesnik, local Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. radio stations. This was not concealed. It was not a secret that this was proclaimed as Serb municipality, that people were appointed. So it seemed ridiculous to us, funny.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, going to a different area, could you briefly and slowly explain to the Chamber the political situation or the atmosphere in Prijedor in 1991 with the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: During the second half of 1991, the war in Croatia was in full progress. From Prijedor, Serb soldiers would go to fight. They were recruited -- mobilised by the municipality of Prijedor to go to Croatia and fight. The representatives of the SDA opposed this mobilisation, and the soldiers from the reserve units of the JNA went to the battlefields of Slavonija, to Pakrac, to Lipik, to parts of Croatia. From Prijedor, journalists would also go and accompany them. The battle of the Serb people in Croatia was glorified. And when the soldiers returned in periods of 20 days, there was much shooting. It would seem that there were a lot of weapons. There was shooting going on. The people, citizens -- population was disturbed by this, the Muslims. The Croats were condemned and publicly blamed for not taking part in that war which was considered by them -- the fact that they should not take part in that war. There was also an atmosphere of distrust that pervaded the area. There was fear. There was shooting. There were provocations going on. So it was an uncertain time for all citizens of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: In brief, what you say is that the understanding or the trust was divide -- was getting lower, and also that there was fear between the major ethnicities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The citizens were very much disturbed. Shooting went on throughout the night. If the shooting went on from the trucks, and if weapons were used and carried in the streets, and if shooting went on throughout the night, even heavy weapons were being used, they were positioned in visible areas, and there were large quantities of weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, who were the people who were going in the trucks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: They were Serbs, Serb soldiers, they were the only ones who had weapons. They went to the front lines in Croatia. I simply want to say that the Serb army, the Serbs were armed, the soldiers were armed. There was a lot of shooting, as I said, was going on. Much weapons were brought back from Croatia. And it was rumoured that the greatest concentration of arms was in Bosnia. There was a growing distrust among the peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, if I take your mind to the period in 1992 before April, what was the political situation that prevailed in Prijedor during that time, if you could state very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "political situation"? I explained that the assembly had not been functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Why do you say that? Why didn't the assembly function?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the deputies of the SDS were leaving the assembly, and very often, the work of the assembly was blocked. The sessions were convened. The meeting was opened, the quorum was established, and then a question was raised that could not be resolved by the assembly. Given that situation, the deputies of the SDS would abandon the assembly of Prijedor. I remember very well that when the Serb deputies left the assembly, all the others left as well. There were 60 deputies remained out of 90. There was also a situation where we had a quorum and we could work. And Cehajic was chairing the meeting, and we said: "We have to stop work because the SDS is leaving." I got up and said: "We can continue with the work. We have a quorum." But the work of the assembly was interrupted. The SDA wanted to continue work, but the misunderstandings were so great that the result was that work was rendered impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: During this time before April, what was the function -- did you observe the propaganda which was in the media?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the propaganda was quite obvious in the sense that the Serbs had to be armed, that they should, at all costs -- that their fate of World War II be prevented, that they should be safeguarded. That they cannot experience the disasters that they experienced in World War II again. It was said that they were killed by the Ustasha, the camps were mentioned where they had suffered. And the remnants of various saints were carried, and there was an atmosphere of preparation and -- in order to avoid the situation occurring, a situation of World War II, the Serbs thought that it was necessary to prepare for war. They didn't want a repetition of the disaster of World War II, 50 years before. This, in fact, was in the Serb press. Belgrade -- papers from Belgrade were read widely. It was said that the Serbs were in danger, that they had to fight for their rights, and this is the way things went.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, you're aware that the takeover in Prijedor municipality was on the 30th of April, 1992? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Before this, during the time that you spent as a member in the Municipal Assembly, did you see Mr. Stakic and know Mr. Stakic well?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I met Stakic after the multiparty assembly was set up. He was a young physician. He comes from an area of Omarska, which is quite densely populated settlement in Prijedor. But before 1992, I didn't -- that is to say, until 1990, I didn't know him. Following the multiparty elections and the assembly, I got to know him because he became vice-president of the assembly of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Before the takeover on the 30th of April, have you spoken to Mr. Stakic when he held the post of vice-president in the Municipal Assembly, before the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Quite sincerely, amongst the deputies, there is a normal communication. I didn't have any specific contacts with Mr. Stakic, but we knew each other. We would greet one another, and he would come to my snack bar for breakfast. I'd see him around town, because he used to be, at the time, vice-president of the municipality in the street where I often went. We knew each other, but we were not in particularly cordial relations. But we knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, now, on the 30th of April, 1992, did you get to know that there had been a change in the power in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: On that morning, when I got up, the workers informed me, the workers going to work informed me, that there was a lot of soldiers in the town, more than usual. And various points -- checkpoints were established in town. A worker told me that she had been stopped ten times. "The soldiers were there at the checkpoints, and I could hardly make it to work. I don't know what is going on." I said to her: "Well, we will probably work anyway, open up the restaurant. I suppose someone will come to have some coffee or fruit juice." I didn't take the situation seriously. This was early. This was around 7.00 in the morning. Then I went down. I went to my house in the main pedestrian area, and my restaurant was across from there. And there, I saw many armed soldiers in town. They were carrying guns, weapons. They were acting in a fairly -- there were posters throughout town. They were not acting very respectful. The radio stated that power had been taken over by the SDS, and this is what I saw happening. At first, I was shocked. In the proclamations which were put up throughout the town, posters were, in fact, put up, and the local radio station kept repeating this, that the SDS had taken over power because it could no longer watch the SDA lead the municipality to economic disaster, to further problems. And the SDA could not resolve all those problems, and that is why the SDS took over power to make life better for the population, to improve the economic situation. And this was repeated on the radio and on the various proclamations in town. Then a Crisis Staff was established. This was rather a cynical thing. The SDA itself did not hold power on its own in Prijedor. The SDA had shared power with the SDS. It also had a part in the power of Prijedor. And to say that the SDA alone led the municipality to economic disaster was both ridiculous and cynical.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, in that last answer, you mentioned about proclamations and posters. Could you very briefly say what you saw in them and what these proclamations were?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, listen, there was a proclamation issued to the residents of Prijedor. I have to say that ten years have passed since, and I can't remember what it said exactly in this proclamation. But here is the gist of it: That the SDS had taken over power because it was unable to simply watch how the SDA and the Muslims led the municipality into economic disaster, heavy economic losses, and et cetera, et cetera. And it was signed underneath by the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor municipality. It was quite strange for me to see this Crisis Staff mentioned for the first time. It was unusual for me. I have to say that the situation in town was also quite unusual. There were many checkpoints with troops on them, on all high-rise buildings, there were soldiers walking on rooftops. So I saw that the situation was serious, and that this takeover of power, regardless how it was said on the radio constantly that the taken over without a single bullet, it still heralded bad times to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you spoke about a Crisis Staff. Did you get to know or was it announced as to who the people who were involved in the Crisis Staff, or who held posts in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Never officially. Never officially. It was never announced who held positions in the Crisis Staff. However, we knew after the municipality of Prijedor was created, the Serbian municipality of Prijedor, we knew and it was publicly announced that people who held leading positions were in the Crisis Staff. Because this Serb municipality of Prijedor was in a dormant state until the takeover of power. Once the power had been taken over, the president of the municipality or the president of the Crisis Staff was the post awarded to Milomir Stakic. This was not publicly spoken about, but we all knew it. And the names of other people who were involved in it were never publicly announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you -- are you aware as to what happened to the people who held posts in the legally elected government and the other members after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these people remained in town. I think the first day following the takeover was Saturday or Sunday. So, a day or two after the takeover, these people, not knowing any better, went to their offices. And since in front of every institution, every enterprise, there were armed soldiers guarding the entrance, they turned back these people. And Mr. Cehajic was turned back as well. It was circulated for a long time afterwards that Mr. Nedzad Seric was turned back from the Court building. He was the president of the Court and a judge for a number of years. He was a very respected man, because his father, his late father, used to work in the municipal administration as well. He was a very popular man, a prominent man in town. And when they turned him back from the Court building, when he was turned back from the reception of the Court building after he was not allowed to go into his office, people started whispering about Nedzad Seric being turned back. Everybody condemned this, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats alike. Nedzad Seric [Realtime transcript read in error "Ceric"], I see his name is spelled here. It should be S-E-R-I-C. So this was a shock, a total surprise that these people were turned back. And a majority of Croats and Muslims were turned back from their offices. They were sent back home. They were not allowed to enter their offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you said that you got to know about the Crisis Staff that was functioning after the takeover in 1992 in April. Who were the people who were in the Crisis Staff according to your information and what is your source?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I think as far as the main people are concerned, their names were publicly known. The president of the Crisis Staff was Milomir Stakic. The president of the executive council was Dr. Kovacevic. In that Crisis Staff, there was also a man who was the secretary of the secretariat of the interior, which was in fact the police, and that was Simo Drljaca. So the people who were involved in the Serb municipality of Prijedor who had been established two months prior to that were involved in it. So we knew it, as far as we could tell, Slobodan Kuruzovic was a member of the Crisis Staff. He was a teacher before the war, and he spent a lot of time on the front in Croatia and later became the commander of the Territorial Defence. So these were the main members of the Crisis Staff, and it was rumoured that there were some military representatives in the Crisis Staff as well, commander of the garrison, Radmilo Arsic, and somebody called Zeljaja. And these were the people who held the most prominent posts. We simply knew them to be people who were appointed by the Serb municipality of Prijedor to various offices within that municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you have information as to when this Crisis Staff met or where they met?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Based on our information, they met at the municipal building. I don't know where else they could have. Because Milomir Stakic was the president of the Crisis Staff, and at the same time, he was president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you hear any announcements or any proclamations made by the Crisis Staff after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: After the takeover, the Crisis Staff frequently made announcements under that name, "the Crisis Staff." They asked the Bosniaks to surrender their weapons. They also asked that the TO posts held by the Bosniak Muslims and villages be turned over as well. They simply issued proclamations through mass media, through radio, and the local papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, did you meet Mr. Milomir Stakic after the takeover? And if you did, where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, I was one of the residents of the town. All of these developments were quite unusual for me, and I went to inquire as to whether we were going to continue working, whether people would be going back to their offices, and how things are going to develop in general. I was interested about our future. So I call the municipality, and the secretary answered. Her name was Mica. That was her nickname. I believe her last name was Radakovic. And I asked her to get in touch with Dr. Stakic. I simply wanted to hear from the first man of our municipality what was going on. She told me to come the following day. And the following morning, I went there at about 9.30. I went to the municipality. I can't tell you exactly what day it was, but it was -- it might have been 3rd or 4th May, so several days after the takeover. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I went there together with several prominent members of my association, Huso Hadzic was with me, Andrea Pavic. I think there was also the secretary of our association there with us, Mr. Simatovic. Mr. Stakic met with us at about 9.30. I joked a little bit with the secretary, with Mica, and I told her: "Listen, Mica, the presidents here keep changing, but you are constant. You are also here. She was the secretary for Mr. Cehajic before. And during the socialist regime, the president of the municipality was Mirko Pavic, and she was his secretary as well. So I told her: "Well, listen, Mica, the presidents keep coming and going, but you are here always." And so we went in Mr. Stakic's office, and Marko Palic came out of there, and we greeted each other because we knew each other. We went to school together. And when we were in Mr. Stakic's office, I asked him openly: "What is this all about? What is this all about? Are we going to work? Are we going to keep our cafes and catering establishments open? Are we going to have fuel? What do you think is going to happen? Nothing is going to change for the better" and so on. And Mr. Stakic looked at me and said: "Well, we'll see. You seem to be not informed." And then he mentioned Kupres. And then he said he didn't really know how the situation was going to develop. And then he told us he was about to go to Banja Luka at 10.00, and that he was going to find out what was going on. And then he told me to come back and see him upon his return. So we stayed there for some 10 to 15 minutes. I didn't learn anything new. I didn't know what was going to happen. Mr. Stakic told me he was going to go to Banja Luka. He didn't tell me who he was going to see in Banja Luka. He simply said he was going to gather information there. And then he said: "We'll see each other, we'll talk later on, and then I'll tell you about it." However, he never called me. Neither did I. So this is where we left it off. And then things started developing very quickly after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask a very simple question from the witness before we take the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, very briefly, when you went to Mr. Stakic on that day, where did you meet him? Did you meet him in the president's office where Mr. Cehajic was occupying?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: The allocation of offices in the municipal building was always the same. As you entered to the left was the office of the president of the municipality, because it was a large office and it also had a conference room. And to the right was the office of the vice-president and it only had one room in it. Mr. Stakic was already occupying the office to the left which was normally the president's office. And this surprised me. And I simply concluded that he had moved into Mr. Cehajic's office. So a day or two later, after the takeover, he was already occupying that office. And it was unusual to me, because I know that he used to have a different office, an office to the right from the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We adjourn; resume at 4.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And we restart immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, when you -- before the adjournment, you said that you met Mr. Stakic in his office. When you went to the municipal building, were there any armed personnel or soldiers present?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in front of the building, there would usually be several soldiers, just like in front of all other buildings in town. It wasn't the case just with the municipal building; there were armed soldiers in front of the Court building, the police building, banks, important institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, with the takeover, what changes did you observe in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in town?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were many soldiers walking around town. They were armed. In front of all buildings, or rather on top of all high-rise buildings in town, there were armed soldiers. One could see them clearly on rooftops. The situation was quite sad. There was a curfew which lasted from 10.00 p.m. until 6.00 a.m. And during the curfew, one could not walk about town. The situation was tense, and I don't know myself, because I didn't walk around town myself. But people were fearful, and it was not a normal situation for our town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know as to who imposed the curfew?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff imposed the curfew. It was clearly announced that the Crisis Staff had decided what the hours of the curfew would be, from the evening until the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were the people able to get to their places of work? Were they able to move freely?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, during the day, people moved about town. However, they did so fearfully. A vast majority of Bosniaks and Croats were turned back from their work. They were not allowed to enter the premises of their companies. By this, I mean socially owned companies. And the situation as I told you was quite tense. The -- there was the curfew, there was a large number of soldiers around town, on rooftops. A lot of troops were armed. My employees complained that soldiers would come in drunk and leave their weapons on the bar or on tables. So it was a situation where many people felt intimidated, were fearful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, during this time, did you come to know of a situation where people had to take a loyalty oath to the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The policemen who were Bosniaks and Croats were required to sign a loyalty oath, confirming their loyalty to the Serb government, the Serb state, as they called it. They had to undertake a written obligation to be loyal and participate in the work of the Serb government. This especially applied to policemen. A vast majority of policemen who were Bosniaks and Croats did not agree to sign this. They were automatically fired from their jobs, and also disarmed. At that time, I have to add that various incidents or various events took place that increased the tension in town. There were several murders that went unresolved. Many instances of revenge took place. There were also cases where people were pulled off buses and killed. A prominent businessman Kutkavic [phoen] was killed in the suburbs. He was pulled off a tractor. Some people were taken off the bus between Prijedor and Bosanska Dubica and killed. And the Crisis Staff was the only contact -- Crisis Staff was the only source of information regarding this. And they explained this as a case where this was a revenge for a soldier that had been killed in town. So the times were very uncertain. There were shootings going on. One couldn't sleep at night from all the shooting that took place, and all of this contributed to the sense of fear among people. So these were uncertain times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you observe the soldiers and the police personnel in the Prijedor town acting in coordination or direction of the SDS or the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: It was absolutely synchronized and coordinated. The Crisis Staff informed about everything as a Supreme Commander would be. The Crisis Staff coordinated the work of the police, and in some ways the army was also involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, I would bring your attention to the 22nd of May, 1992. Do you recall an incident at Hambarine at a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was on the 21st or 22nd of May. I don't remember exactly. There was an incident at the checkpoint held by Bosniaks, by Muslims. Hambarine, where the incident took place, and six villages or six local communes, which prior to the war were inhabited by over 10.000 Bosniaks, organised their own Territorial Defence. And in some ways, they tried to protect their own villages. They did not leave their villages; they remained in Hambarine. And at one checkpoint, which was on the road to Ljubija, another settlement, there was an incident where there was some shooting as a result of which one Serb soldier was killed. This incident, I think, took place on the 22nd of May, and the Crisis Staff addressed the population regarding this, requiring all of those who participated in that incident to surrender themselves. They mentioned a name of some commander in Hambarine, some Aliskovic, yes Aliskovic. Therefore, the Crisis Staff wanted him to surrender himself to the Serb authorities. They believed him to be personally responsible for the death of this Serb soldier. Naturally, the Bosniaks refused to surrender, and the Crisis Staff issued an ultimatum to surrender all weapons and to have those soldiers, as they called them, surrender to the Serb authorities. So this was what the ultimatum was all about. This ultimatum was broadcast throughout the entire day on the 22nd of May. It was broadcast through the local radio. I have to say that for a long time prior to that, we were unable to listen to any other radio except for that local station. We were unable to watch Belgrade television or Sarajevo or Zagreb television. The only one available to us was the Banja Luka television and the one in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You said that there was an ultimatum which was broadcasted. What happened after the ultimatum expired?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Next day, there was a terrible shelling and bombarding of the village. The shelling, the bombardment from all sorts of weapons, lasted almost the entire day. There were even some tanks that crossed the bridge over the Sana River and moved in the direction of the Hambarine village. The regular forces of the army were also involved so this was terrible. And for the very first time, it was then that we were confronted with the artillery, the artillery was left in villages, in -- where the Serbs lived. So the shelling lasted a long time, and there was much destruction in those villages and severe civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, what was clear from this sequence of events, after the Crisis Staff made an ultimatum and when it expired, the attack by the military?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: It was obviously that the Crisis Staff and the army and the police, that they worked in coordination because the ultimatum was issued by the Crisis Staff, and that the -- and the army, with its tanks and heavy artillery, attacked the village. So we knew that all this was very much planned and coordinated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, did you -- were you aware that subsequently, an area which is known as Kozarac was also attacked?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a few days following the attack on Hambarine, which, to be quite honest, did not meet with any special resistance. There was vast destruction and people saw that their homes were being destroyed and that people were being killed and they were very much in a state of shock. A few days later -- this was, in fact an unselective shelling of homes in the village. A few days later, an ultimatum was issued that Kozarac, too, that the TO of Kozarac, should also surrender its weapons. I must say that Kozarac is in a different area of the town from Hambarine. 12 kilometres from Prijedor in the direction of Banja Luka. And it is not a village. It is a small town. It used to be a municipality. It is composed of four local communities. And before the war, about 19.000 Bosniaks lived. A very small percentage of others, of Ukranians, and Croats and others lived there, too. But 95 per cent of the population were Bosniaks. And then an ultimatum was issued to Kozarac, according to which Kozarac was to surrender its arms, and that the TO should surrender. The ultimatum was also issued by the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor. And it was even demanded that the police should disarm. And then terrible shelling ensued, and bombardment with heavy weapons, tanks, cannons of all calibres against Kozarac. This was not done in a selective fashion. From my own apartment, from Prijedor, I could see that from all directions, in the direction of Kozarac, shells were being fired. Firing took place from different spots in the direction of Kozarac. I'm not an expert in military matters, but we nevertheless could see how the rounds flew over us in the direction of Kozarac. In the case of Kozarac, I could also say that the ultimatum was issued both to the police and the TO. The police in Kozarac was basically of Bosniak ethnicity. Unfortunately, the police surrendered at that time, together with the commander, and none of them have been found nor have been exhumed. They apparently were all killed. The commander of the police station was Mahmuljanin. I don't remember his name exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, now I would take your attention to a different area. When were you first arrested? And briefly, how did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was arrested the first time on May 23rd. It was a Saturday. I was at home alone. I was watching television. Unfortunately, we could only see the programme -- the Serbian programme of Banja Luka from 7.00. At one moment, the speaker -- the presenter said -- the announcer said, when reading out the news: "A group of extremists from Kozarac admitted that the financing of Bosniaks, Muslims, that they were financed by a well-known caterer, someone from the restaurant business in Prijedor. His name was Murselovic. And there was also Dr. Kulenovic mentioned. Someone who I did not know at all. I was truly shocked when these names were mentioned on television. At that very moment, I called the police, the policeman on duty answered. And I said my name. And I said that information was given on the news, on television. "And what is this all about? Can you give me an explanation? This is wrong information. Can you explain it to me?" A policeman by the name of Jankovic answered the phone. I knew him personally. He was a junior policeman. He told me: "I don't know anything about it. Don't you worry." I called him first on phone, and then I went to the premises, to the police building itself. Because it is quite near from my home. It was still daytime. It was 7.00. And I went there, and I said: "What is going on? Please deny the information, the truth of this information. I have nothing to do with this. Don't drag me into things that I have nothing to do with." He told me: "You go home. I know nothing about it. If we need anything, you will find out soon enough".

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, were you a member of any resistance group at any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you ever finance the Kozarac TO or the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for five or six months I hadn't been to Kozarac. I didn't even pass through it. I had no special links at the time with Kozarac. I had never financed -- well, I joked on that account. I said that if someone asked some advice from me, I would give it willingly, but I was not in a position to offer money.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, after this announcement, you went to the police station and came back. Thereafter, were you arrested immediately and taken to the police?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, half an hour later, I was at home -- perhaps 20 minutes, 40 minutes. I don't know exactly. But about half an hour or so had elapsed, and then someone called from the pedestrian street, called my name from the pedestrian street, since my office there and everyone knew I was there at the time. I sit there, watch television, read or write something. Someone called out my name. I opened the window, and I saw two policemen who said that I should prepare, get ready, and come down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were the policemen in their police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, two policemen. There were two policemen. One of them was Bato Kovacevic. That was his surname. I knew him well. The other one, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was the arrest to the Prijedor police station?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kovacevic, Bato was his nickname. I don't know what his real name was, we called him Bato Kovacevic, he was a policeman at the Prijedor police station. Through the window, I told them I had been to the police and there was no need to call me. They told me to come down and to follow them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you go with them and were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They didn't ask me anything then until I reached the police station, the secretariat of the interior. It was a building about a hundred or 150 metres from my apartment. And then they took me to an office in the police building. It was on the second floor. The person who interrogated me was a young investigator. I think his name was Krneta. He asked me: "What do you know about that?" And I told him I know nothing about it. What I learned is what I learned from the news, and that this was a case of wrong information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did they detain after you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: They detained me. Krneta, well I told him I have no connection with this. I wanted to go home. They didn't let me go home. I was on the second story in an office there. And I remained there until 12.00, half past 12.00. I was there from 7.00 more or less. I asked to return home. I was sitting on a very uncomfortable chair for three or four hours. They didn't give me anything to drink, not even a glass of water. I asked to go home. I was asking why I was there in the first place. I protested. And they told me that I could -- that I should sleep over at the police station. "Does that mean that I'm under arrest," I asked. And they said: "Yes, something like that."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And where did you spend the rest of the time in the police station?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I left the office on the second floor, it was number 30 or 34. I think the -- I saw that someone else was being brought to the police building. Ilijaz Music, a professor who used to work with me at the school. And we were taken down to a building in the yard. We were closed, shut there. This is a place where people were closed, shut, if they were caught drunk. It had bars, iron bars, pretty high. And there, I saw several people who had come there like me. There was Music and there were several more people whom I knew. I saw Mehmed Tursic, the head of the internal revenues department of Prijedor. I said I saw Music, Dr. Sikora, a young physician, a Croat. And someone called Juso Seric, a tradesman, who is employed in the Naftagas company. And a young man who worked -- who was about 20, 25. He worked at a restaurant where one of my colleagues worked. We were talking. We were wondering why we were there. We were all civilians. After about half an hour, all of a sudden, the doors opened, and the president of the assembly, Muhamed Cehajic, entered. I tried to joke with him, and I said: "We are in good company, high-level company. We have the president with us." And while we were there in this building in the yard, the police were charging, unloading, loading their guns, and they were shooting, firing, and bullets were being fired. And some of them were even fired in the direction of our building, and they kept saying: "These are Ustasha, they should all be killed." So we had to move away from the window. And we spent the night there in that premise. We were standing or sitting. We feared the shooting that took place from the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You mentioned a person by the name of Music, Ilijaz Music. Did he hold office in the SDA? And what --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He was a member of the top leadership of the SDA. And to tell you the truth, we knew each other. We used to work together previously. I also went to secondary school with one of his brothers. We were the same age. So he was in the top leadership of the SDA, and he was even one of the Bosniak candidates for the president of the municipality. However, within the party primary, Cehajic won more votes, and at least this is what I heard. But at any rate, he was one of the prominent members of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Ilijaz Music thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: When I was released the following day around 5.00 or 6.00 p.m., I never saw Music after that. So I was released, and I never saw Music afterwards. And the following day, or on Monday, which was the first business day -- the first following business day, I got a call from his brother Dr. Music, who told me he had heard that I had been together with his brother, arrested. So he inquired about his brother, because his brother went missing. And I told him what I knew. I told him that I had seen him, but that I didn't know what happened to him afterwards. I didn't know whether he remained there or was released. And then Dr. Music, the older brother of Ilijaz Music, told me: "I'm going to look for him. I will go to the police and the municipality tomorrow. This is ridiculous. What have they done to my brother?" And later on, I learned that this doctor, in fact, did that, and went missing every since. I never heard -- I never heard from him or saw him ever again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: He was a professor, Professor Ilijaz Music. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a professor of physics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the name of Mehmed Tursic. Have you seen him since?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, frankly speaking, yes, I did see him. Later on, when I came to Omarska, and after about some ten days, a bus came in, as usual. It was bringing prisoners to Omarska. And he came in the same group with the president of the Court, Mr. Nedzad Seric. And I saw him leave the bus, and then kept seeing him for several days in the camp compound, because we would see each other when we ran to lunch. However, three or four days later, I didn't see him any more. But I did see him initially when he came to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know whether he survived the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: He did not. That's definite. Because later, at the end of 1992, I met with his wife in Zagreb. She left for Sweden in a convoy from Zagreb. She left at the end of 1992 or later on. And then I met her when she came to Prijedor in 1998 and 1999. And at that time, she told me that Mehmed Tursic on the 23rd of May was arrested, and then released. And then arrested again and taken to Omarska, and then she lost trace of him. So he wasn't seen from -- he wasn't seen later on, and it is certain that he had been killed in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. Mehmed Tursic, what position did he hold in the SDA, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what was his position in the organisational structure of the SDA. But the SDA appointed him as the director of the internal revenue agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: The two people whom you mentioned Mehmed Tursic and Ilijaz Music, to what ethnicity did they belong to, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: They were Bosniaks. Bosniaks and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You mentioned about another person, Dr. Sikora. A medical doctor. Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you about him. He was a young physician. I knew him very well because he frequented my restaurant quite often. He was very open and social and friendly. I never saw him subsequent to that arrest, the one that took place on the 23rd of May. And the following day, when I was released, his mother came to me, because the rumour had circulated that we both had been arrested. So his mother came to me to inquire about her son. I couldn't tell her anything because I didn't know anything. I told her that I had been released and that he probably remained there. And then I took her in my car to where she lived near the hospital in Urija. I never saw his mother afterwards. I met his father, because he was in Omarska camp as well, and I used to speak to him there often. He was an elderly man, some 75 or 76 years of age. He went to Omarska and Manjaca, and later on he was released and I don't know what happened to him afterwards. But their son, Zeljko Sikora, I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And you mentioned another person, Muhamed Cehajic. This was on the 23rd of May, 1992, when you saw him in the cell in the SUP building. Did you see him thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: When I was arrested for the second time, I saw him in Omarska on the 30th of May. So seven days later. He was in Omarska in the same room where I was. When we came to Omarska in the evening hours of the 30th, this is when I was arrested for the second time, I saw him sitting on the tile floor, and he had a beard. He was unshaven, and I simply could not comprehend that he had been sleeping for seven days on a tile floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him thereafter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Since we were in the same room, I saw him there a lot. I spoke to him a lot as well. He stayed with us in that room for some time, and then he went to Banja Luka for some questioning. He even showed me some kind of a draft indictment charging him for something. He spent some 10 or 15 days in Banja Luka at the most. And afterwards, he came back to our room. He said that it wasn't bad for him in Banja Luka. They gave him enough food, cigarettes. He was a passionate smoker. And he was very pleased with the treatment he had received in Banja Luka. So he stayed with us for some time in a situation where there were 700 of us in one large room. Later on, he was taken out and I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You spoke about Dr. Sikora. Do you know to what -- what ethnicity he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Zeljko Sikora was a Croat. He was a Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you said that you were released the next day. Could you explain very briefly as to how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: When they brought me back from that small cell where we had spent the night, back to that inspector who was called Krneta, on the 24th of May in the morning, he, who was a young man, told me that he was married to a Muslim woman and had a child with her. I knew his father. I had worked with him many years ago, 20 to 30 years ago in a national park. His father was a forester. And I managed to establish rapport with him. And at one point, he told me: "Listen, Murselovic, the Crisis Staff had denied the information that it was announced over -- there was announced on television regarding you." And I was extremely pleased to hear that, and I asked him: "Well, why don't you let me go, then?" He said: "Well, I can't do that, but we'll see what's going to happen to you." And then I remained in that office until 4.00 or 5.00 p.m. Some policemen came then, Mejakic came, Drago. They even gave me some food. They treated me fairly decently. And then they took me to see Ranko, Baja. His last name was Mijic. He was the head of the Criminal Investigation Department in the police. I knew him. He was a bit younger than me, maybe some ten years. So I told him: "Baja, what's going on? Why was I arrested?" And he told me: "You will be released." And I said: "Why am I here to begin with?" And he said: "It's fine. You are going to leave this place." And then he asked me if I had any intention of leaving town, and he -- he wanted to know whether I would remain in Prijedor, in case they needed something, and I told him even if I wanted to leave Prijedor I would be unable to because the town is completely blocked and a bird couldn't leave it unseen. I told him that my family was in Belgrade, having left town some five or six days prior to that. And I told him that I perhaps might go to Belgrade myself. And he said: "Okay, we'll let you go this time. However, you may not leave Prijedor. You have to remain within our reach." And I was released at around 5.00 or 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you said that Krneta, the officer who had spoke to you before you spoke to Mijic, said that the Crisis Staff had denied the information. Did he say from whom he had got the news?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. He simply told me that this is what the Crisis Staff had said. He said that that information regarding me had been denied, and that that was a positive move. He didn't tell me anything else, and that was quite enough for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Then you spoke about a person by the name of Baja, or Baja is a nickname and his family name is Mijic. He was a police officer attached to the Prijedor police station?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He was the head of the Criminal Investigation Department. And he was in charge of all these investigators and inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see him thereafter when you were detained in the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I saw him come to Omarska, and I even meet him now in Prijedor. I saw him seven days ago in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, my question was the time you spent in Omarska during your detention, did you see Mr. Mijic come into the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know for what purpose he was there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all prisoners who had been brought to Omarska had to go through some interrogation, through some questioning. And he was sort of in charge, and I suppose since he was the head of that department, all of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these investigators, inspectors, were subordinated to him. There were many investigators there who came daily on a bus in the morning. And they used to investigate prisoners. This is how we called it. And I was interrogated as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you again arrested on the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. The police arrested me again on the 30th of May, in the morning around 11.00 or 12.00. They banged on my door. A neighbour of mine in a military uniform, Ranko Vujasinovic, a young man, banged on my door. He was wearing a police uniform. And he told me: "Well, it's quite unsafe here. There's some shooting going on, and why don't you go across the road to the Hotel Balkan." There were several other policemen with him, and all of us, all of my neighbours, Serbs and Bosniaks, there were elderly people there, we all went across to the Balkan Hotel, and we sat in a cafe there, for at least three to four hours. Prior to that, they asked me whether I had any weapons, whether I had a pistol and so on. I told them I had a pistol and a license to carry it. They asked me to surrender it to them. I went back to my apartment, took my pistol, my license, and turned it over to this neighbour of mine, Ranko Vujasinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So you handed over the pistol and the license to the person who came and asked you to come out of the house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And what uniform did he -- was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: They were wearing police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you know whether they were policemen? Was he a policeman?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: He wasn't a professional policeman. They were reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that you and there were others taken to the Hotel Balkan. Who were the others there at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: There were lots of people from my neighbourhood there. Many of my neighbours were there. Many people I knew were there. They were brought from all parts of the town. And we sat there in the hotel not knowing why we were there. We heard that there was much shooting going on, and we were told that we should stay there because it was a safer place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Then what happened thereafter? Were you taken anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Then they said that the Serbs should remain, and that the Croats and Muslims should separate to another side, and males under 60, and that we should line up. And when these groups separated, we were ordered to leave the hotel. There were some buses waiting. They were waiting before, even before. And we were taken into those buses. Of the people I knew, there were quite a number of them. And I remember Sefik Terzic, Kiki, who was a barber. Asef Kapetanovic, who was in the restaurant business. There were not very many of us in the bus. About 20, maximum 25 people in the bus.
