utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... when they were ordered to get into the bus?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The young policeman, the reserve policeman, by the name of Vujasinovic, Kiki Terzic, the barber tried to ask a question to find out where we were going because he used to know that person. He was on friendly relations with his parents, with his father, Sveto, and the barber had a barber shop nearby. This was all in the centre of the town. And this young man used to go to the barber shop frequently with his parents. And the barber used to know him quite well. Well, this young policeman kicked this older man and told the driver: "Drive this shit."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you beaten at this instance?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no one beat me then. But when we started moving, we actually started from the Balkan Hotel to the Mose Pijade Street, and the post office, and then we turned right to the post office and the police station. On the Zebra Crossing [phoen] which separates the municipality and the police, the bus stopped. And the policeman, who entered the bus with us and who was armed and whom I knew quite well, I forgot his name. It may have been Grahovac, I'm not sure. I knew him nevertheless. I asked him: "Where are you taking us? Why are we in the bus? Where are you driving us?" And he shrugged his shoulders and said:"I don't know". When the bus stopped, I asked him can I go out and go to the police station and see what is going on? Why are you taking us? Why have you arrested us? "Well, if you want, you can go out," he told me. Is there a commander there? Is Drljaca there? Is Jankovic there? Who are these people? Why are you argue us? Where are you taking us? I found this to be strange. There were older people there, civilians, businessmen. It was quite unusual, abnormal. Well, I left -- the policeman let me go off the bus. I went in the direction of the police station to find out what was going on, to protest, simply. And facing me was a soldier who was coming in my direction. I think that he had some military insignia. And he asked me where I was going. "Sir, I do not know you," I told him. I see that people are being arrested. They are being taken somewhere, and I don't know what is going on. I wanted to ask the commander what was going on and why we were being taken. He didn't know me. He was not from Prijedor. Had he been from Prijedor, he would have known me. He asked me what my name was. When I said "Muharem Murselovic," the person was amazed. "Well, you are those who are slaughtering Serb children. Go back." He kicked me in the behind, and I jumped into the bus. And then he got on to the bus with me, and he said: "You are the ones who want to slaughter our Serb children. Lie down," he told me. And then we all laid down in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, did you observe as to the buses, the buses which were used? From where did these buses come from? Were they Autotransport buses?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: They were state-owned buses, owned by the state company Autotransport. Some had names. These were usually transport lines in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: City of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the city of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did anybody accompany the people, the people who were in the bus? Were there armed guards?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: In that bus, in my bus, there was an armed policeman, not a soldier, an armed policeman who stood next to the bus driver, near the entrance to the bus. And he kept us there. We were lying face down in the bus, and when we had moved away from the town, then he felt sorry for us, I suppose, and he told us to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, where did the bus ultimately -- where did the buses go to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all the buses headed for the Partizanska Street. It's in the direction of the village of Gomjenica. When we got up and sat down, we saw that we were heading towards Gomjenica. And we drove for about half an hour. And then we went to Sanicani -- Tomasica. And then we reach the Omarska area, because Omarska is between Prijedor and Banja Luka. But we entered the area from the other direction, the mine. I had never been to that mine before. I didn't know it. I had no reason to go there before. It was an iron ore, the Ljubija iron ore in the Omarska part, the Tomasica part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this was the 30th of May, 1992. How long did you stay in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from May 30th, I was in Omarska. We saw that it was a camp, that there were guards there. And that lots of things were happening there. I stayed there until August 6th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, coming to the Omarska camp and spending almost more than two months in the camp, could you briefly state the specific areas that you were detained in the camp? The names of these places, as popularly known.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I spent about 70 days in the camp. And the room where I was put, it was called Mujo's room. It was behind the restaurant. It is the place where the wardrobe used to be, the cupboards were pushed to one side. And the room -- well, I was practically all the time in that room with the exception of a few days when I was taken to an area called pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, could you describe the Mujo's room to the Chamber, as to how the dimension of the room.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: That room, well, you entered it from the side. Well, its dimensions were 15 by 12, more or less. 12 in width; 15 metres in length.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When you were first to the Mujo's room, on the 30th of May, 1992, how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, in that room, well, there were not very many people there. Ten, 15 people maximum. Very few people. And here, I met Mr. Cehajic, president of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And approximately how many people would you estimate would have been there in that room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it varied between 200, 300, up to 600 or 700. We were in rows, like sardines. Some people were being transferred there. But on the average, there were about 500 people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And were the -- did you know the ethnicity of these people who were detained in that room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the people were familiar to me. They were for the most part Bosniaks, Muslims. But there was a fair number of Croats, too. But a lesser number than the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see a person by the name of Stipo Sosic in that room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Sosic, yes, he was there, too. He was a Catholic priest from Ljubija. I didn't know him before, but he greeted me and asked me how I was. And the -- he said where his parish was. And then we were frequently in contact. He was detained there, too. There was some other Croats, 5 to 10 per cent of us were Croats. There weren't more. There was a musician I knew, a music professor. His name was Ivica Peretin. There was also a driver and his son. They were also Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you ask Stipo Sosic as to why he was detained there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I had no idea why he was detained. He was detained because he was a Croat. I didn't even know why I was detained, let alone I didn't know why the priest was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: In time passing, what was the condition of the prisoners in Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the conditions in the camp, in the whole of the camp, were inhuman. We slept on tiles. Who had a piece of cardboard or some paper, well, he was considered to be privileged, not to have to sleep directly on the tiles. Who had a coat would spread out his coat and lay on the coat. Simply, these were not normal conditions in all respects. As regards food, well, we were fed once a day. And 30 of us were crammed together. And in a very brief period of time, we had to run from pista to the kitchen to take the food, which was poured out there, to eat that food very quickly. And even quicker than that, we had to run and return the plate. It was usually spoiled food, beans or potatoes, swimming in something like water. And we were usually beaten on the way out because sometimes, we would spill some water and oil, so that if we slipped, we were met by the people on guard and we were beaten. We drank water from the Banjanica [phoen] River. It was not drinking water. It was industrial water. And many of us suffered from dysentery, from stomach diseases. And many people who refused to eat food were constipated, so they were unable to go to the toilet for as long as 30 or 60 days. I didn't go for 30 -- over 30 days. Simply, in our room, well, some of us were set aside, and the excrements were, in fact, all over the place. So all this was swimming there and next to that, were the detainees, sitting crammed together. It was very ugly, very sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were you provided with medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No, we were not given any medical care. There were many problems in that some people had chronic diseases like diabetes and so on, and they had to go without medication. Allegedly, there was a doctor in the camp; however, he never saw detainees. And after all the beating we'd received, the only medication we had available were cold compresses that we would put on our body to alleviate the results of all that beating.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be a convenient time to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us have a break of half an hour now. That means resume 5.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated, and let's continue immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you described the conditions that prevailed in the camp and what you observed during your stay or your detention in the camp. Were you also detained in a place called "garage", during the latter part of your detention?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I spent two or three nights locked in there. I slept, and I lived in something that we called a garage. It was a room whose dimensions were 5 by 4 and a half metres, something like that. And there was to the side of the other room where I spent most of my time, the so-called Mujo's room.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be permitted to tender an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: From the set of exhibits that was submitted as S15, in the index, it's 9 E, and ERN number 00409596.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would be, then, 15-3. Correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections? Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a photograph from the model of the Omarska camp. If the photograph could be moved a little bit to the right. I want the photograph -- the Exhibit Number 00409596 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 9592 we had already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I'm told, Your Honour, that this photograph -- the exhibit is S15-2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it. I had the impression we had this before. It's indeed dash 2. We had this already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Witness, would you look at the exhibit which is on the ELMO, please. You said that you were detained first in the room we just called the Mujo's room which is in the restaurant building. On this photo could Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you kindly point out the building which you called "the restaurant building" please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: This was the main entrance here, in this area here, the area that's protruding. And it had -- it was covered by a roof. And then this circular part is the staircase that leads to the first floor. This here was the area that all of us called Mujo's room, this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was this the building --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: And then there's an entrance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was this the building which was called the, "restaurant building"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: This is behind the restaurant. The restaurant is right up here in front. This is the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Then to assist the Chamber, could you also show the place that you referred to as the "garage," the entrance to the garage.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Right here. This area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: This was the room that you said that it was 4 by 5 metres in size?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, there was another place that you referred to in your evidence earlier as the pista.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This whole area here, between the hangar, the entrance. So this entire area here we called the "pista." It was all covered in asphalt, and we called it the pista.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How would someone enter Mujo's room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can see the entrance here on this side, right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What is the white building which is on the edge of the picture?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: This one here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: This was called "the white house."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you also could see another small building away from the white house. Do you know as to what it was called by the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: This one here. Well, this here was the white house, and the other one, I don't know what it was called. Thank God, I never went either to the white house nor to the other one. This other one was a red house or something like that. But I never went there. I never went to the rooms there in 1992. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, what is the big building which is opposite the restaurant building? Do you know as to what the prisoners called this big building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this large building was called the hangar. They had workshops there to repair heavy machinery, dampers, and the machinery that they used to load and unload the ore. And they were quite large, so this entire area was called the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Were prisoners detained in the hangar building, too?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. The prisoners were in this entire area, this one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I have the assistance of the usher to have the exhibit 00409597 be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it correct, this is a new one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then this is 15-3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No objections. Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. This would be S15-4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. There was a mistake. There was an exchange of the pictures, and the former dash 2 remained, of course, dash 2, and now we are only with dash 3. The other was not used --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: The other was not used. That's right. Thank you. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, is this a picture of the restaurant building from the model of the -- Omarska model?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This here is the restaurant, as I told you. This is the entrance, and this is the staircase leading to the floor above.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, do you see the door on the side which also -- which enables someone, anyone to enter the -- anyone to enter the Mujo room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And also at the extreme end, could you find out the place where you called -- the place that you called the "garage"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Murselovic, also before we take the photograph away, would you be able to show in the picture where the interrogations were held?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: The interrogations took place up here following the staircase, there was a hallway, and offices on both sides. So this up here were the offices where the interrogations took place. So you would take the staircase, and then once you got up there, there was a hallway, and offices were to the left and to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: It was in the first floor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: A person who would enter the restaurant for meals, would you be able to show as to how one would enter the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: During the day, in accordance with a predetermined schedule, we would go to have our meal. And that lasted from 9.00 a.m. until 6.00 p.m. we would line up here in this area, and since we were close to the entrance of the Mujo's room, then 30 prisoners would line up and then run through this main entrance to enter the restaurant. This was a self-service restaurant, a typical one. And we had to get our food very quickly, as I told you, the food was bad indeed. We would also take one-eighth or one-quarter of a loaf of bread. We would eat it quickly, take the plates back to where we picked them up originally, and then usually take the same way back, running along it, and then get through the door back to the pista and line up there. This whole process lasted not more than 3 minutes. So lining up, running, getting the plates, getting the food, eating, putting the plates back, and running back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Is it correct if I say that people who would go for the meals from the front door of the restaurant would be in the pista area for some time before they go for the meal?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. We would line up here in groups of 30. And only 30 people were allowed to go in for their meal. And this is why this whole process took so long, because there were many of us. So sometimes we would eat at 10.00 in the morning and sometimes at 5.00 p.m. Because only 30 people were allowed to line up in a group, and then enter the restaurant and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Is it correct if I say that you were only given one meal a day?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was just one meal a day given to us. It was a bad meal at that. You could hardly call it a meal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Murselovic, when you were detained in the garage, the place that you call the garage, the latter part of your detention in Omarska, who were the people who were with you whom you could recall the names, whom you could recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can recall a number of names. People's names were called out in accordance with some preselection by the investigators -- or I don't know whom. Dedo Crnalic was with me. Nezir Krak. Sefik, Kiki, Terzic, Dr. Sadikovic. So there were a lot of people. There was even one woman among us. There was some hundred and 50 to 170 people in the garage with us. There was a woman called Hajra there as well. She never left the camp. She must have been camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: There were many prominent people. Enes Kapetanovic. It has been ten years, but still I was able to give you names of six, seven, eight people. We were all crammed in that limited space, and this is how we spent our nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you mentioned the name of Kapetanovic. Is it Enes or Asef?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: It was Enes Kapetanovic. And he's a relative of Asef Kapetanovic. Asef Kapetanovic was taken out previously, and he was not in the same room with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You also mentioned about a woman being detained with you by the name of Hajra. Do you recall the family name of this person?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I think the last name was Hadzic or Hodzic, although I think it was Hadzic Hajra.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: And you said that she never left the camp. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Because immediately after that -- well, there was some 30 to 35 female prisoners in the camp. I can't tell you the exact number. But around that. And all of those women, among whom I knew many, there was a lady judge there, Nusreta Sivac. There was a lady called Besirevic Mugbila [Realtime transcript read in error "Basirovic"]. She was an economist. She used to work in a bank. There was an employee of mine there, Avdic Sadija. Then there was Hajra. Then there was Medunjanin. No, it was not Medunjanin. There was a lady, Mahmuljin, Velida who was a teacher. There was Jadranka Cigelj there as well. There were many women that I knew from before there. And a few days prior to that, a bus had arrived with investigators, and these women were taken back to Prijedor. I later learned that they were allegedly taken to Trnopolje or Prijedor. However, three or four women remained, and there was no trace of them thereafter. Hajra was among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a person by the name of Velida Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Have you seen her since the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I never saw her again, but I knew her very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did she hold any office or position in the assembly or the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: She was a deputy of the municipal assembly of Prijedor, and she was there on behalf of the SDA. Otherwise, she was a teacher by profession, and she used to work for some time in Kozarac. Her husband, his name was Suleja Mahmuljin, and he was a dentist by profession. And her family name was Arnautovic, maiden name. And she came from the part of the city called Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You also mention the name Basirovic as in the transcript. But is it Mugbila Besirovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mugbila Besirevic, she used to work in a bank. She was an economist. She came from Cejreci, a local community quite near the town. She was an elderly lady. She was very active in her local community. She was highly respected by the people, and she was one of those who never left the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What you say is that she did not survive the camp, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, she did not survive the camp. She never left Omarska with the other colleagues when they were returned to Prijedor after having spent 50 or 60 days there. And all traces of her were lost. No one heard of her any more. Her family never heard of her, her children. And I saw her husband when I left Omarska after the war. He lived in Bihac about eight months. Following that, her husband unfortunately also died.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you mentioned about Hajra Hadzic or Hodzic --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: -- Being detained in the garage with you in the latter part. Where were the other female detainees being kept?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: During the day, they used to sit in a corner of the restaurant. Some of them would help around when food was being served. They would hand over the bread or food. During the night, they were taken to the premises on the floor above, and we had no contact with them during the night. So we didn't know what was going on during the night. We don't know under what conditions they were living there. But during the day, when we were having our meals, they would sit in the corner of the restaurant. This was frequently the case. They would clean the area, the floors. They handled the dishes. But in most cases, in 90 per cent of the cases, they would sit quietly in that corner and that is how they spent their day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, taking your attention to another area, could you explain the times that you were beaten in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that during the interrogation which lasted about 30 or 40 minutes, I was, in fact, one of the last to be interrogated after having spent 30 days in Mujo's room. Muja, the police, took me up the stairs, and during this questioning, I met Ratko Milosavljevic there. He interrogated me. He worked at the assembly as an agriculture engineer before. He took me to a room which was on the left of the staircase. On that occasion, I was not beaten. I was interrogated by two persons. I think one was called Nenad, and the other one Neso. They used to be investigators, I think, in the police before. On that occasion, I was not beaten. They asked me some questions. They didn't have much sense, where I was, where I had been, what I had been doing. I told him that I had been arrested once. Then one of them went to ask someone what to do with me. I think one of them was tall and one of them was short. He said I should be interrogated like all the others. I wasn't beaten then. I was beaten three or four times on later occasions. Once, I was beaten by the guards in pista where we used to sit after having our meals. It was very risky to go and have the meal because then we would have to stay on pista, and then we were exposed to the guards. Then Kevo Simo came on one occasion, and said: "Look, here's Mursel, he used to persecute Serb children when he was employed at the school." Well, I had not worked at the school for 14 years then. But the person recalled that. He used to work at the same time as me, when I used to work at the school. And the guards then took hold of me. They started beating me. Well, with cable, with batons, longer than police batons. I was beaten on the pista itself. They said: "You persecuted Serb children." And a blond policeman called Marmat was the roughest amongst them. Marmat was his surname, and it was familiar to me. I had many students from the area, and these are strange surnames. They don't end in "ic" which is mostly the case. Their names were Marmat, Vuceta [phoen] And so forth. And people who worked in the school remember those names of the other teachers. Two policemen beat me fiercely indeed. I tried to defend myself. I was in a crouching position. And I think Marmat was the worst of all. At one moment, I saw red, and I told Marmat: "Ask Borka whether I persecuted Serb children." When I mentioned the name Borka, he just Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. stopped. He recalled the name. It may have been his relative, his sister. And at that moment, they stopped beating me, and they said: "We'll see about that." Then Kiki Terzic was the target of the beatings, and they let me go. But before that, I was severely beaten on the head and on the shoulders. This was one occasion. Then on another occasion, I met Marmat again in the restaurant. He was standing behind the counter. And he shouted to me: "Mursel, where are you?" And I turned around because on those occasions, you just looked straight ahead of you. You don't turn right or left. Then I saw Marmat, and I just couldn't help asking him: "Did you check up on what I told you?" I was referring to Borka and the fact that he said I had persecuted Serb children. He said: "Well, sorry," he said, "that is something I experienced." This is one occasion when I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, in your detailed description of that beating, you mentioned the name Kevo Simo. Is it Simo Kevic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Was he a guard at the camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. I don't know what his business was there in Omarska. And unlike the others, he was wearing an army uniform, an SMB, olive-green uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you were beaten again severely once when you went to get your meal.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was some unwritten rule in the case of the guards that they would -- they simply spilled a bit of oil and water, and since we were running we frequently slipped and fell. Once on my way back, I was running, and there were some young fellows behind me. One of the guards was standing alone. And he hit every prisoner on the head or on the shoulders with his baton. Sometimes, there were five or six of them who beat the prisoners. But on that occasion, there was one guard who beat absolutely everyone who passed by. He hit me on the ear. And then the boys behind me pushed me, and I fell because I had slipped. And I slipped on my knees, and I hit the door. And the pain was very intense, because I was hit. Then the boys got up. I had felt a pain in my foot, and the guard I hadn't met before, he collected his wits about him. He hit me while I was lying down, ten times with the baton -- with the thick cable. I was standing alone. There was no one behind me, so he was able to beat me very hard indeed. I was able to run the 5 or 6 metres and join the other prisoners. Well, about 15 minutes, I was trying to get up, and he kept beating me, so I can barely muster the strength to cross over to the other prisoners. This was a fortunate thing for me because someone came and helped me up. And when he saw in what condition I was, he said: "Well, he is useless." They tried finding some younger men to do some work. I was left alone. Two young men were taken to do some work. They were taken somewhere, but they never returned. And therefore, I was not killed. Once, I was also beaten when I went to the toilet. It was in the hangar. I wanted to go to a toilet because the other toilets were filthy. You couldn't even approach them. The conditions were inhuman. The toilets were blocked, and people said that the toilets were better in the hangar. And when I went there, someone broke down the door, one of the guards, people I didn't know. And they said: "Oh, you're a balija, a Turk." They said something offensive. "You're washing yourself." I was crouching because they were these crouching toilets. They started beating me, and they, in fact, broke my ribs. I managed to stand up, to pull up my trousers, and to rush out, to lie down on pista. But about two months, I felt the consequences of the beating. I had trouble breathing and eating. I put some compresses on my ribs, but the consequences were long-lasting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, when these beatings took place, were the guards, or the people who were there in authority, present?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were all there. They would pass by. It was clear -- perhaps this was not organised, but it was supervised by them. The guards were allowed, I would say, to do what they wanted with these people, because the people that beat me, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, now, coming to the area of the people who were in charge of the camp, did you get to know or observe as to who was in command of the camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the man who introduced himself as the commander of the camp was Zeljko Meakic, and his assistant was allegedly Drago Prcac. He was an elderly man, a retired policeman. And there was Kvocka there, as well. I can't remember his first name. He was married to a Muslim lady, to a lady from Crnalic. At least that was the rumour circulating. There was a man called Kos. We used to call him Krle. In fact, he was a former student of mine. I thought him during my first year of employment as a teacher. There was a man called Krkan. I think his first name was Mladjo. He was a chubby man. And then there were some other people. I can't remember their names. Kos was the shift leader. And shift leader was, so to speak, in charge from, say 7.00 a.m. To 7.00 p.m. The shifts were usually 12 hours long. And the shift leaders were in charge of policemen there. In addition to that, there were people who would come every day to investigate or to interrogate the prisoners. There was a man that I had mentioned previously called Baja among them. And these people were either professional policemen who had worked up to 1992 in the police like the man who interrogated me, Mijic and so on, but in addition to that, there were also people who subsequently became active and prior to that used to be reserve policemen, for example, Dragan Radakovic, who prior to the war was the director of the national park. He was an art teacher before the war. And I also mentioned Ratko Milosavljevic who was an agricultural engineer and used to work for the municipality and so on. There were many people there, people of many professions who became active. It was also rumoured that some interrogators came from Banja Luka. They were looking for certain information and so on. So these are the people who were in charge at the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, now, you mentioned people coming for interrogation. Did you see them coming to the camp for interrogations? How did they come?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: People would come by buses. The buses would normally park on the pista. People would be taken out. And usually, while entering the camp, they would be fiercely beaten. And they would beat them at that first entrance when they searched them, looking allegedly for weapons or I don't know what. I just know that they severely beat these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, if you didn't understand the question, I was asking about the people who came to conduct the interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I apologise. Those who came to conduct interrogations would come daily on a small minibus. It was a minibus that belonged to the iron ore company Ljubija. It was driven by a chauffeur from either the Autotransport company or a chauffeur from the mine. I knew him. So this minibus would come at about 7.00 a.m., and the interrogators would normally stay there until 5.00, 5.30. We would see them as they left the bus and as they boarded the bus to go back to Prijedor or wherever they lived. So they came daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Murselovic, you said that you used to see Mijic who worked in the police before coming to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: When he came to the camp for interrogation, do you know as to what post or position he held in the Prijedor police?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: He was the head of Criminal Investigation Department. So he was a boss to all of these civilian inspectors, if I can call them that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Other than Mijic, did you recognise any other police officers who came for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've told you, among those who interrogated me, there was -- there were two of them called very similarly, Nenad, Neso. And I can't remember exactly their names, their last names, even though I still see them in Prijedor now. One was short and the other one was tall. But it has been ten years and I can't recall that now. They were professional police workers prior to that. And they would come regularly, daily, and conduct interrogations. There was another man there, Drago Mejakic. I would see him as well. So these were the people that were police employees before the war as well. But there were those who would also come on that minibus to interrogate people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: The guards in the camp you mentioned in Omarska, what uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: They wore police uniforms. They usually had blue police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see the commander whom you mentioned, Meakic, in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We saw him through the window when we ran. He moved about the camp freely. He was some 15, 20 years younger than me. He was somewhat tall, blond, a handsome man. And he acted as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he wore regular police blue uniform, the light one. On one occasion, they took us out at night, and he was there. Together with a policeman called Brk, and maybe some others. So they took us out at, perhaps, 1.00 a.m. I was taken out together with Dedo Crnalic, Kiki Sefik Terzic, and it was so pitiful, so ridiculous. They told us the following: "See how poorly dressed the Serb policemen are, they don't have good uniforms. So why don't you give them some money so they can buy some uniforms. You are well-known entrepreneurs, we know you are successful businessmen. Why don't you give them 10.000 deutschmarks so we can get them some good uniforms." So you know, when somebody takes you out at 1.00 a.m., you can imagine what fear we felt. And then how cynical it is to ask the prisoners to buy uniforms for their guards. You didn't know whether they were joking or it was some kind of a provocation. I kept quiet the whole time. I didn't say anything. And then Meakic addressed me, and then he said: "Well, listen, Mursel" -- because this is how everybody called me -- "you're a smart man. You always come up with great ideas so how come you don't have a good idea to solve this right now? And I told him: "You take me out at some wee hour and then you want me to come up with good ideas. Why don't you take us to Belgrade." Because I knew what they were hinting on. If we go there, we can send you money from there, and then they sent us back to our room to sleep and this is how it all ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you said you were interrogated and they asked you questions. Did they ever tell you why you were arrested and why you were detained?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: They never told me anything. And right at this minute, I remembered what the last name of one of those interrogators was. His last name was Tomcic; his first name, Nenad. So to go back to the other story, they kept me on a chair, a three-legged chair, for many hours. And I was there with a slice of bread that I picked up during lunchtime. I have to say that they treated me decently. Nobody hit me at all. They asked me where I spent that week between my first release until my second arrest, from the 23rd until 30th. I told them I was in my apartment, and I did nothing wrong. And you should know this better than me. And then they asked me something concerning the assembly, concerning Cehajic. They asked me whether Cehajic asked money of me. I told them: "No, he didn't. I don't have money anyway," along those lines. So this lasted some 30, 40 minutes. Nobody hit me. They simply asked me where I went, what I did, whether I'd financed the SDA. I told them I had not been a member of the SDA, nor did I finance them. They asked me about my contacts with Cehajic. I told them he was the president of the municipality and I had a good rapport with him in the assembly, which was quite normal. And...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, after you left the camp or the time that you were in the camp, did they initiate any proceedings in a court of law?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No. They did not initiate any proceedings. And during the interrogation, I did not sign anything. They simply told me: "Go back to where you were." And I went back downstairs, because the interrogation offices were on the first floor and we stayed on the ground floor. And I asked them to give me a policeman who could escort me downstairs because it was very typical for policemen to beat people who they were interrogating. You could hear terrible screams during interrogations. So these two interrogators who interrogated me gave me a policeman who escorted me downstairs to where my fellow prisoners were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: After your interrogation, were you released immediately?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: No. This was perhaps some 30 days into my stay in the camp. And following that, I stayed there for another 40 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, now, you referred to in your evidence about beatings that took place during the interrogations. Did you observe or see anybody being beaten or being brought after being beaten when you were detained in the restaurant building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: As we sat the entire day in that Mujo's room, this so-called interrogation went on during the whole day. People were simply beaten up. You could hear the sounds of people being thrown against the wall, thrown on the floor. You could hear screams mixed with painful moans. And it became impossible to listen to those screams, which came from a floor above. We were downstairs. It was terrible. And some people came back from interrogation during the daylight. I remember that several people were so severely beaten that they died in our room. For example, Zijad Ziko Mahmuljin, who was an economist, he was the president of the executive council of the municipality at one time. He was sent back after this so-called interrogation, and he passed away shortly thereafter, an hour or two later. And then there was a man called Camil Pezo. He was the director of an agricultural station. And he had also been beaten and came back in a terrible shape. He died an hour after that. He still gave some signs of life, but he and others had arms and legs that were so injured that we couldn't really do much for them. And they would die, and we would simply take them outside of our room. An old man, Safet Ramadanovic, who was also a caterer, was severely beaten, too. They beat him, perhaps not as intensely as the others, but he was so old and in such a poor physical shape that that was quite enough for him. He developed dysentery, like a vast majority of others, and he also died in our room. The president of the court, Seric, was also beaten on one occasion. His arms were severely injured. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. However, he was not in such a terrible shape after that. There was a man there called Crnkic. He was an engineer and used to work in the mine. I can't remember his first name. His brother was called Husa. He was the principal of the secondary school and was also killed in Omarska. So this man was quite strong, was built quite strong. And we put compresses on him for a day or two, wet compresses, to make it wet. And he was black and blue all over. However, physically, he was strong. I just remembered his first name. Esef, Esef Crnkic. And all of a sudden, I saw that he had bumps, bumps coming out all over his body, on his head. You know some bumps were bigger, some were smaller. It was a terrible sight. He was a terrible sight. I asked Dr. Mahmuljin, I said, "Osman, tell me how come that this man is developing these bumps all over his body and head after the beating?" And the doctor replied to me and said: "He will die soon. His kidneys and his liver are detached now. So all the liquid, all the fluids in his body are running loose. And this leads to this deformation of his body." So this man was employed in this mine previously, and what a tragedy that now in the same mine he met his death, and he used to be a leading engineer. And he was brought to the same premises where he was interrogated and beaten. And he was not the only one to meet this fate. There was Sarajlic, who was a member of the board of directors of this mine. And then there was another man who was an economist and was a prominent manager in the mine. And another man whose name I cannot remember right now. So these people, these people gave a large share of life to building this mine. And then later on, the fate would have them be imprisoned and killed in their own company later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, you mentioned the president of the court, Seric. Is his first name Nedzad Seric?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned the name Nedzad Seric. He was a lawyer and president of the court. He was there, and he was beaten also.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you mentioned about another person by the name of Dr. Osman Mahmuljin. Did he survive the camp?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM MURSELOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't survive the camp. He was severely beaten before coming to the camp, before he was brought to the camp. He was beaten thoroughly, and his arms were black and blue from top to bottom, both arms. This doctor, who was a good friend of mine, who was my own physician, he simply couldn't bring his fingers together, join them together. He was a person that I held in very high esteem, whom I liked very much. He came to the camp about 20 days or a month after I had come. And he was in such a state of shock, he couldn't even imagine being a prominent doctor and head of a hospital. He was a specialist in internal medicine. And the witness to his marriage. He married -- he was there, a witness to the marriage of some person from the SDS, whose name was Simo Miskovic. He was a witness to his marriage, and this is something that is much respected. If you call him to be your witness, this is a great privilege for someone. And this was a shock to him. He was conscious of his status, and he was very much affected by the beatings, that something like that could happen to him. There was also another physician, doctor, there, Dr. Reso [as interpreted] Sadikovic. He was an ORL specialist. He was a very popular person. He was very funny. He was humorous. He appeared in the local press. He had a column there. He would write articles. He was present there, both him and Osman. One evening, they were taken out, and they never returned. I remember the exact moment when Esad, Esad Sadikovic, when he was taken out. He was called by Dragan Prcac. This was between 10.00 and 11.00 p.m. It was dark. There was a bus parked on pista. And he said that Dr. Sadikovic should come out. He was in our group. And he was confused, and very much intimidated. He asked: "Should I take my things along with me, my belongings?" And Drago Prcac said: "If you want to, take them with you. If you don't, you don't have to." Esad said farewell to all of us, we exchanged kisses, he left and I never set eyes on him again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
